analysis.one_liner: Swept away most federal, state, and local phone and cable regulation and let phone companies sell TV without local franchises.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate Commerce Committee until the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced nearly all existing telephone and cable regulation — federal, state, and local — with a single new federal framework. Phone companies could have entered the TV business without negotiating a franchise with each city, cities could not have capped video fees above 5% of revenue, and no government could set rates or require companies to share their networks except in narrow cases. It kept a few consumer floors: a capped basic phone rate, federal quality standards with small fines paid to affected customers, a ban on internet providers blocking lawful content, and faster number transfers.
analysis.who_benefits: The largest telephone companies, which wanted to sell video nationwide without negotiating a franchise with every city; cable and satellite operators, which would be freed from local franchise terms and buildout requirements; and mobile carriers, which would be shielded from regulation unless the FCC found competition lacking. Competitive phone companies would gain less: interconnection would be set by private contract, and the requirement to share copper lines would be weaker and end in 2011.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big phone, cable, and satellite companies

how_it_helps.text: A video provider could not be required to obtain a state or local franchise, follow any buildout mandate, or lease its facilities to rivals, letting phone companies roll out TV service city-by-city without local negotiations.

No federal, state, or local government could regulate the rates, terms, price, or quality of any communications service, or force a network owner to share its facilities, except as the bill itself provided.
The FCC would generally forbear from regulating mobile services, and states could not regulate direct-to-home satellite service at all.

Cities that wanted to build their own communications network would first have to publicize the plan and give private companies the right to bid to provide the service on the same terms, with ties going to the private bidder.

Incumbent phone companies would keep obligations to offer capped-rate basic phone service and to provide competitors unbundled copper loops, though the sharing obligation would expire January 1, 2011.

analysis.who_pays: Local governments would lose most franchise authority, see video fees capped at 5% of gross revenue, and be limited to four public-education-government channels; state regulators would lose rate and quality oversight and keep only enforcement of new federal standards; subscribers would lose class-action rights and see penalties for service failures capped at $500 per household; and after 2010 basic phone rates could rise with inflation. City-owned broadband would face a private-bidding gauntlet.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip states and cities of authority over rates, quality, and franchise terms, replacing enforceable local consumer protections with federal standards whose violation carries a fine of no more than $500 per household — and no private class actions would be allowed.

While barring providers from blocking lawful content, the bill would expressly let broadband providers sell 'customized plans' that differentiate access to content and availability of applications — a legal pathway for tiered, pay-for-priority internet service.

The 'safety net' basic phone rate cap would exclude subscriber line, universal service, and similar fees and taxes, and after January 1, 2010 carriers could raise the capped rate by the CPI each year.

Municipally owned broadband networks would be subject to an open bidding process in which any private company could claim the project on the same terms, with preference to the private bidder in a tie — a hurdle that would make city-run networks far harder to launch.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered genuine simplification of a regulation-by-technology patchwork, and its basic-phone cap and quality standards were real consumer floors. But its core was deregulation whose benefits flowed overwhelmingly to the largest network owners: local franchise authority, rate oversight, facility-sharing duties, and the municipal broadband option would all be swept away, with subscriber remedies capped at $500 per household and class actions barred. Consumers might have gained more video competition, but they would have paid with weaker local accountability and a built-in legal route to paid-priority internet plans.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Ensign, joined by Sen. John McCain, introduced the bill on July 27, 2005, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Sixteen Republican senators cosponsored the bill.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history — and the bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, incumbent cable operators kept their local franchises longer, and state and local governments kept their authority over rates, quality, and rights-of-way. Big phone companies continued to negotiate video entry market by market rather than gaining a national franchise-free pathway.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbent cable companies and local regulators

for.name: Sen. John Ensign
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it as its Senate sponsor.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.what_they_did: Joined Ensign in introducing the bill.

for.name: Bell telephone companies
for.role: Incumbent local phone carriers (Verizon, AT&T and peers)
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress in 2005-2006 for a national video-franchise framework that would let them sell TV without city-by-city franchise negotiations; this bill was the most sweeping version of that rewrite.

against.name: Sen. Ted Stevens
against.role: Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled S. 1504 for committee action; the committee pursued its own, narrower telecom rewrite (S. 2686) in 2006 instead.

against.name: State and local governments and municipal-broadband advocates
against.role: Franchise authorities and city-network operators whose powers the bill would preempt
against.what_they_did: Objected publicly to federal preemption of local franchise, fee, and municipal-network authority during the 2005-2006 telecom rewrite debate.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored the bill, and no vote was ever taken, so the opposition's partisan shape was never recorded.

industries.industry: Incumbent Bell telephone companies (Verizon, AT&T and peers)
industries.note: The bill would let them sell TV nationwide without local franchises, escape most rate and facility-sharing regulation, and curb their main municipal competitors. Their gain came largely by removing state and local oversight that protected subscribers.

They would gain freedom from local franchise terms, buildout mandates, and PEG-channel obligations beyond four channels, but lose the franchise system that had kept phone companies out of their markets.
States and cities could not regulate direct-to-home satellite rates, billing, or equipment at all.
The FCC would have to forbear from applying most regulation to mobile services unless competition or public safety required it, with petitions deemed granted after a year of inaction.

Any city wanting to build a network would have to expose its plans and let private companies bid to take over the project on identical terms, with ties going to the private bidder — making publicly owned networks far harder to start.

They would keep unbundled access to copper loops, but at 'commercially reasonable' rather than cost-based rates, and the obligation would end entirely on January 1, 2011; interconnection would otherwise be set by private contract with little regulatory backstop.
